items.title: PM Carney welcomes ‘any moves’ to restore free trade, Hoekstra predicts deal could come soon
items.description: Canada and the U.S. could reach a deal on trade before the end of 2026, American Ambassador Pete Hoekstra predicts, but don’t expect the midterms to move the needle.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Left: U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra. Right: Prime Minister Mark Carney. (The Canadian Press)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Canada and the U.S. could reach a deal on trade before the end of 2026, American Ambassador Pete Hoekstra predicts, but don’t expect the midterms to move the needle.
items.body:
Canada and the U.S. could reach a deal on trade before the end of 2026, American Ambassador Pete Hoekstra predicts, but don’t expect the midterms to move the needle.

Hoekstra, who was appointed as Washington’s ambassador to Canada by U.S. President Donald Trump, made the prediction during an interview with commentary outlet Northern Perspective.

“I think Mark Carney probably knows exactly what he wants, the president knows what he wants. They’ve got to iron out a few of those differences,” he said.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Asked whether a Democrat-controlled Congress will influence negotiations, Hoekstra said he didn’t think it would. “The president knows what he wants to get done on trade. I think that’s exactly where he’s going to keep driving,” said the ambassador.

On Tuesday, Democrats celebrated sweeping victories across the U.S., taking both the House of Representatives and the Senate. In doing so, they captured the majority of congressional seats, solidifying control over the American legislative branch.

Prominent Democratic senators have rallied against Trump’s tariffs on Canadian imports, especially in states that rely on trade with Canada to bolster their domestic economies.

For example, Senator-Elect Abdul El-Sayed – who won his race in the auto-manufacturing hub of Michigan – called the trade war “insane” during a post-victory interview with CNN on Thursday.

In Maine, a popular tourism destination for Canadians that relies on agriculture-sector imports, tariffs featured prominently during the campaign. The democrat victor criticized the Republican incumbent for not pushing back against Trump hard enough.

Carney hasn’t spoken with any of those newly elected Democrats about legislation to drop tariffs.

“Obviously, we welcome any moves to restore a free-trading arrangement,” he said in response to a reporter’s question in Winnipeg on Friday. Free trade is in the interest of American families and workers, he contented, and Canadians.

Trump’s tariff authority

But, while tariffs may be unpopular among the new Democrat caucus, Trump’s executive power over trade policy means Congress will face an uphill battle to change his course.

“The swing in Congress, the results of the election, are very unlikely to have a significant impact on the president’s trade agenda and the tariffs that are in place,” Blake Harden, managing director for trade policy at Ernst & Young’s Washington Council office, told Reuters.

“This is because there is so much trade authority within the executive branch that’s been delegated by Congress.”

Once Democrats take control of Congress in January, they could introduce legislation aimed at reining in some of Trump’s tariffs. Trump, however, retains presidential veto powers that can only be overridden with two-thirds support in both chambers of Congress.

Securing a two-thirds supermajority would require significant support from Republicans. While Democrats have secured majorities in both chambers, those majorities are far from the 290 House votes and 67 Senate votes needed to override a presidential veto.

Democrats would also need at least 60 votes in the Senate to overcome any Republican attempts at filibustering proposed legislation.

With files from CTVNews.ca journalist Daniel Otis and Reuters

items.title: Poilievre accuses government of cooking books on immigration
items.description: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says the government is hiding the facts on the number of newcomers it’s bringing to Canada, despite the focus in the new immigration levels plan on people who are already here.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, centre, speaks at a press conference at a food bank in Brampton, Ont., on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Nathan Denette]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Nathan Denette</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says the government is hiding the facts on the number of newcomers it’s bringing to Canada, despite the focus in the new immigration levels plan on people who are already here.
items.body:
OTTAWA -- Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre on Friday accused the government of hiding the facts on the number of newcomers it’s bringing to Canada, despite the focus in the new immigration levels plan on people who are already here.

In Winnipeg on Friday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the one-time permanent residency measures in the levels plan are about making longtime temporary residents permanent.

But Poilievre said at a news conference in Brampton, Ont., the current government is blowing past the Trudeau government’s immigration numbers with plans to grant permanent residency to 200,000 temporary residents this year, in addition to the broad target of 380,000 permanent residents.

“It will bring the total number of new permanent residents to 650,000, by far a record and much bigger than any of the years when Justin Trudeau was prime minister,” Poilievre said.

“We love immigration for people in numbers that we can absorb, where there are jobs, health care and housing, but not when the numbers exceed our capacity to absorb people. It is not fair to immigrants. It is not fair to people already here.”

Carney said the workers expected to receive permanent residency under the new levels plan are people who have been in Canada for years and whose workplaces apply annually to renew their permits.

“They are members of the community, as I say, and they are in many respects -- in all respect -- permanent residents of the country and we’re formalizing it,” Carney said Friday.

Immigration Minister Lena Diab’s office declined a request to interview her about the newly tabled immigration levels plan. She also did not take questions after the plan was tabled on Thursday.

Diab did not face any questions on the levels plan from the opposition during Friday’s question period, despite being in the chamber on a day when many MPs are on their way back to their home constituencies.

Immigration department officials said during a not-for-attribution technical briefing Friday that the vast majority of those eligible for the one-time plan to shift 200,000 people to permanent residency are already in Canada.

That one-year program will select, in collaboration with the provinces and territories, 100,000 people here on work visas who already have applied for permanent residency.

The other 100,000 applicants will be chosen from humanitarian permanent residency streams. Government officials say this is meant to clear a decade-long backlog of applications.

Those applicants include about 32,000 former Hong Kong residents who came to Canada through a special program to flee persecution from the Chinese government, and nearly 19,000 Ukrainians who came here through a program for those fleeing Russia’s invasion.

“So these are people who are not permanent in terms of the classification, but are effectively permanent residents and we’re recognizing that,” Carney said. “It’s the right thing to do and we are absolutely clear about that, and it’s within the context of a sustainable immigration system.”

Andy Wong, president of the Canada-Hong Kong Link, said this is welcome news for those who came to Canada on the Hong Kong pathway.

“It’s even better than we expected because we thought, like, maybe they would try to have a one-time measure gradually for three years to take care of backlog,” Wong said. “So that is a very pleasant surprise and we absolutely are delighted.”

He extended thanks to the Liberal, New Democrat and Conservative MPs who called for expedited permanent residency for those who came on the Hong Kong pathway.

Roy Lee, a former Hong Kong resident with a permanent residency application, said those using the pathway program aren’t technically refugees, but rather people who came to Canada after the Chinese government cracked down on pro-democracy demonstrators in Hong Kong.

“We may return to Hong Kong without any sentences,” Lee said, adding that those who fled the Chinese city fear someday crossing “the red line of the Hong Kong government.”

“So what we are afraid of is the hidden, invisible bottom line that we may somehow reach it in the future and maybe we will suddenly get sentenced,” he said.

Department officials say this humanitarian permanent residency program will include about 45,000 family admissions for spouses, common law partners and children, plus about 12,600 people who have been approved for permanent residency on humanitarian grounds but whose applications have not been finalized.

The stated goal of this program is to reduce application wait times to the 12-month target.

The government says the broad pool of 380,000 permanent residents will be chosen mostly from people already in Canada on work and study visas, with some successful applicants coming from outside the country.

Poilievre also said the Temporary Foreign Worker Program should not be open to communities with unemployment rates higher than 5.5 per cent.

The government signalled in the budget it intends to reform that program in collaboration with the provinces, but the plan is light on details at this point.

There are restrictions in place on low-wage temporary worker applications in census metropolitan areas where unemployment is above six per cent.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

items.title: Champagne, Carney travelling across country to sell federal budget to Canadians
items.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney and his cabinet ministers fanned out across the country Friday to sell Canadians on their latest federal budget — while the Conservatives sought to portray the document as a costly spending binge.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Minister of Finance and National Revenue Francois-Philippe Champagne and Prime Minister Mark Carney arrive in the House of Commons on Parliament Hill to table the federal budget in Ottawa, on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Justin Tang]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Justin Tang</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney and his cabinet ministers fanned out across the country Friday to sell Canadians on their latest federal budget — while the Conservatives sought to portray the document as a costly spending binge.
items.body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and his cabinet ministers fanned out across the country Friday to sell Canadians on their latest federal budget — while the Conservatives sought to portray the document as a costly spending binge.

Speaking at a news conference in Winnipeg alongside Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, Carney highlighted his government’s pledge to end homelessness in Canada within a decade.

“For decades, governments and communities have tried to address this crisis. Too often, these efforts have been inadequately resourced, poorly co-ordinated and not sustained,” Carney said.

“We are investing an unprecedented $30 billion in a co-ordinated national plan. We understand both how difficult this will be, but equally how imperative it is that we succeed.”

The budget sets aside $11.2 billion over four years and $17.8 billion over 10 years for the effort. The federal government says some 65,000 Canadians are currently homeless.

Carney and Kinew unveiled a new partnership tied to the budget to build about 2,000 units of transitional housing and to fund a new mental health and addictions centre in Winnipeg.

Kinew said Carney has put nation-building at the centre of his government and there is no greater nation-building project than “building up the people of Canada” by tackling homelessness.

“Full credit belongs to the prime minister for saying we want to build the housing to end homelessness in Canada,” Kinew said. “No one in a country as rich as Canada should ever be homeless.”

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne went to Montreal on Friday for an event hosted by the Montreal Council on Foreign Relations to promote the federal spending plan, which sets aside billions of dollars to stoke investment.

In his speech, Champagne said the homelessness initiative and the productivity “mega deduction” that lets businesses deduct new investments are the two budget measures that will have the greatest impact in ten years’ time.

Champagne has presented the budget, titled “Masters of our Destiny,” as an ambitious plan to help Canada gain a solid economic footing in an increasingly volatile world.

“It’s about being more resilient, more independent, stronger,” the finance minister told reporters Friday.

“When you’re stronger, whatever happens south of the border, whatever happens in the Middle East or elsewhere in the world, you’re just more resilient. That’s really what I wanted to [have] Canadians understand when we say ‘masters of our destiny.’ There’s something profound about that.”

Opposition leaders have argued the budget falls short, particularly when it comes to helping people struggling with the high cost of living.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre described it on Friday as a “costly credit-card budget” full of “wasteful spending” that will drive up national debt.

“When you put more money on the credit card, you pay more interest to the financial institutions,” Poilievre said. “The Liberals should have called their budget ‘Mastered by Debt.’”

Poilievre made the comments while speaking at a news conference at a local food bank that is facing supply shortages and a spike in demand.

Food banks across the country are under pressure as households grapple with the high cost of living.

“We’ve gone beyond a food crisis to a food emergency,” the Conservative leader said. “People cannot afford to eat. This is the inflation hell that people are living in after 11 years of Liberal government and it’s getting worse.”

The budget includes a pledge to renew a local food infrastructure fund. The fund would provide money to food banks and other aid organizations to both buy food and upgrade facilities, such as greenhouses, kitchens, and transportation equipment. It’s a $124 million investment over three years, starting in 2027.

The Conservatives and Liberals already have sent out fundraising notes to supporters with competing narratives about the new fiscal plan.

The Liberals said the budget will facilitate economic growth and make life more affordable for Canadians, while the Conservatives said the “out of control” spending will lead to higher taxes.

In question period in the House of Commons on Friday, Conservative finance critic Michael Chong accused the government of allowing interest costs on the national debt to “skyrocket.”

“It is the fastest growing expense in the government’s budget,” Chong said. “What is the government going to do if we face another crisis like we did in 2008 and 2020?”

Parliamentary Secretary Ryan Turnbull replied that the government has charted a course that remains within its fiscal guardrails.

“We’re balancing the operating budget one year ahead of schedule and sticking to our debt-to-GDP ratio declining path,” he said.

Unlike Carney’s first budget, which was tabled under a minority government, the Liberals now have a majority and can get their agenda passed without the support of other parties.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

— with files from Maan Alhmidi in Brampton, Ont. and Morgan Lowrie in Montreal

items.body:
Lululemon Athletica Inc.’s chief executive has named two new leaders to her C-suite.

Heidi O’Neill has appointed Ben Hallam as the Vancouver-based apparel company’s new chief brand officer and Emily Sunderland as its incoming chief strategy officer.

Hallam most recently served as senior vice-president of marketing at Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts and joins Lululemon on Monday.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Sunderland, formerly with Boston Consulting Group, will start at Lululemon on Nov. 23.

The changes come about two months after ex-Nike executive O’Neill took on Lululemon’s top job in September in hopes of revamping the business, whose stock has been sagging as competition rises.

Roughly one month into the role, she named a new president and chief product officer as well as a new chief operating offer. Lululemon says her hunt for chief technology and communications officers is continuing.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

items.title: Joly asks Competition Bureau to probe Stelco deal after CEO comments
items.description: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is asking the Competition Bureau to examine whether Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. acted in bad faith when it acquired Stelco Inc.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Industry Minister Melanie Joly and a Stelco flag in a combination photo. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld/Nick Iwanyshyn]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is asking the Competition Bureau to examine whether Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. acted in bad faith when it acquired Stelco Inc.
items.body:
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is asking the Competition Bureau to examine whether Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. acted in bad faith when it acquired Stelco Inc.

In a letter to the competition commissioner, Joly pointed to Cleveland-Cliffs chief executive Lourenco Goncalves’ testimony at a U.S. congressional hearing in January 2026 where he said the company acquired Stelco in part to prevent Canadian steel from flooding the U.S. market.

Joly said the CEO made similar claims to CBC News last month, indicating the company’s disregard for fair competition in the Canadian market.

“For the workers at Stelco’s facilities in Hamilton and Nanticoke, this was a shocking admission, as it was for the government,” Joly said in a statement posted on X on Friday.

Joly said in her letter to the Competition Bureau that it “may wish to thoroughly examine” Cleveland-Cliffs’ conduct and whether it warrants enforcement action under the Competition Act. 

The bureau had reviewed the takeover deal in 2024 and issued a no-action letter, but the minister is now prompting more scrutiny “in light of new evidence regarding the intent of the firm’s conduct.”

Cleveland-Cliffs did not respond to a request for comment.

Stelco announced plans on Sept. 28 to lay off up to 500 workers at its Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., steel mills, citing U.S. tariffs, weak demand for Canadian steel and competition from imported steel products.

  • Latest updates on company news here

However, Cleveland-Cliffs and the union have more recently confirmed only 175 workers have been laid off so far, all in Hamilton. 

In an Oct. 22 letter, Joly had accused Cleveland-Cliffs of championing U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel despite its commitment to support Canada’s steel industry, then using those same tariffs to justify axing jobs.

She demanded the steelmaker make good on the job commitments it made when it bought Stelco and gave the company 15 days to respond or face potential legal action from the federal government. 

The layoffs have fuelled an escalating, and very public, dispute between Joly and Goncalves.

Last week, Goncalves said he hopes to recall all workers before Dec. 25 if a plan to boost sales of Canadian-made steel to domestic customers succeeds.

Joly’s letter to the Competition Bureau on Friday came on the same day as Ottawa’s 15-day deadline for Cleveland-Cliffs to address the layoffs. 

  • Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.ca

If the company fails to comply with its employment commitments, Ottawa has said it could ask a court to order it to meet its commitments, pay penalties of up to $10,000 a day or force a sale of Stelco.

Michael Guglielmin, Conservative MP and chair of the Conservative Steel Caucus, pressed Joly to deliver on her promise to sue the company.

“It has now been 31 days since Minister Joly sent her first letter to Stelco, promising legal action if they didn’t reverse their layoffs,” he said. 

“Now she’s sending a fourth letter, shifting accountability to the competition commissioner.”

Ritika Dubey, The Canadian Press

With files from Brett Bundale in Ottawa

items.title: President Peña skips Senate impeachment trial as Paraguay reels from Ueno bank collapse
items.description: Paraguayan President Santiago Peña failed to appear for his impeachment trial in the Senate on Friday despite promising to defend himself in person.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Paraguay President Santiago Peña speaks to the media at United Nations headquarters, Sept. 19, 2023. (AP Photo/Ted Shaffrey, File)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Ted Shaffrey</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Paraguayan President Santiago Peña failed to appear for his impeachment trial in the Senate on Friday despite promising to defend himself in person.
items.body:
ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguayan President Santiago Peña failed to appear for his impeachment trial in the Senate on Friday despite promising to defend himself in person, as lawmakers moved toward a verdict that could remove him from office over the dramatic collapse of a bank tied to his administration.

Peña is accused of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno Bank while regulators overlooked risky insider lending. The central bank’s seizure of Ueno this week sent shockwaves through Paraguay’s financial and political system and locked nearly 3 million customers out of their savings, prompting mass demonstrations.

Senators voted 39-3 to reject Peña’s request for another 72 hours to prepare his defense. He said he received the summons only hours before the session, along with some 300 pages of accusations and evidence, which left him no time to review the case. Presidents impeached in recent years in other countries, including the United States and Brazil, have had weeks to prepare.

  • Latest updates on international news here

The Senate wrapped up closing arguments late Friday afternoon and moved to a final session to deliberate and vote on whether to remove Peña from office.

His lawyers, Ricardo Preda and Adolfo Ferreiro, argued that senators should have accepted the resignation that the president submitted Thursday instead of pressing ahead with the trial. Opposition lawmakers insist Peña be removed through impeachment to be held accountable, a choice that could decide whether he retains immunity from prosecution.

“He must go, but not home. He must go to a maximum-security prison,” opposition Sen. Yolanda Paredes told reporters. “The public is fed up with impunity.”

Under Paraguay’s Constitution, elected presidents who resign receive a lifetime Senate seat that comes with parliamentary immunity. Prosecutors have already opened criminal investigations into the bank’s collapse targeting Peña, current and former central bank and pension fund officials and Vice President Pedro Alliana, who is next in line for the presidency.

Public outrage has become more thunderous by the day. Thousands of protesters demanding their frozen savings back and accountability for Ueno’s failure have clashed with police firing rubber bullets and pepper spray this week. Paraguay’s largest teachers’ union, which has more than 40,000 members, plans to begin an indefinite national strike Monday to press for protection of public pension funds.

“This was an enormous betrayal of trust,” said Yinal López, a worker at the state electricity company, whose employee pension fund also had money at Ueno. “The president made a mockery of the people. He used their money, the people’s money, to do whatever he wanted.”

A bank collapse becomes a political reckoning

Ueno’s implosion has plunged Paraguay into its deepest political crisis in more than a decade — and at dizzying speed. Regulators seized the bank before dawn Tuesday. By Thursday afternoon, Peña had offered to resign as his conservative Colorado party turned on him, led by former President Horacio Cartes, the party chief and Peña’s longtime mentor. By Friday, his interior minister, chief of staff, legal adviser and political adviser had all quit.

It was a staggering reversal of fortunes for Peña, a telegenic technocrat and former International Monetary Fund economist who owed his rapid political ascent to Cartes. The tobacco magnate, among Paraguay’s richest men, made Peña his finance minister and twice backed him for president over rival factions’ objections.

Once in office, though, Peña quietly amassed a rival power base, analysts say. Ueno Bank, flush with public deposits, became the centerpiece of both his business empire and his effort to win over provincial governors as he sought to escape Cartes’ shadow.

“It’s like a Shakespearean drama. He tried to displace his mentor, his political patron,” said Miguel Carter, director of DEMOS, a Paraguayan research center. “But he did so on very fragile grounds.”

Cartes struck back. In September, senators loyal to him demanded answers from the central bank about Ueno’s lending, citing leaked internal reports that warned its loans to related companies put its solvency at risk. When Ueno collapsed this week, so did Peña’s leverage, and Cartes, once sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury over alleged corruption, publicly called for the ouster of his erstwhile protégé.

“Cartes put the nail in the coffin,” said Andrew Nickson, a Paraguay expert at the University of Birmingham. “Peña had no political base to rely on, and he was left high and dry.”

A bank built on public money

Ueno rose from obscurity to become Paraguay’s fifth-largest bank by deposits in just a few years, with more than US$800 million in public money turbocharging its expansion. It signed up more than two-thirds of the country’s adults, its splashy logo appearing everywhere from the national soccer stadium to street vendors’ bank cards.

The impeachment charges cite Peña’s stake in Ueno’s holding company, which he divested under pressure last year, and his appointment of a former Ueno executive to run the central bank that regulated it. Lawmakers also accuse him of letting the state pension fund deposit US$355 million at the bank, beyond legal limits.

Analysts say those high-level connections helped shield Ueno from regulatory scrutiny even as concerns about its finances grew.

“For the last 20 years, the central bank has been one of the two pillars that gave Paraguay international credibility in managing its economy,” said José Tomás Sánchez, a political theory professor at the National University of Asunción. “And under Peña, it began to lose credibility, lose neutrality and then relax all its control mechanisms to favor the business group that had Ueno Bank as one of its pillars.”

Frozen accounts, rising anger

Overnight, Ueno customers could no longer withdraw cash, access their savings or use their cards to buy anything. The digital lender had aggressively courted the poor and unbanked with generous supermarket rebates, and more than 1 million Paraguayans opened their first bank account there, according to Ueno. Even players on the national soccer team, which Ueno sponsored through its run to a World Cup upset of Germany this year, say their accounts are frozen.

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

“The ripple effect on the general population has been immense,” Nickson said. “That has fueled the ire of many people in Paraguay who are not particularly politically aware or very interested in politics.”

Some depositors began recovering their money Thursday, starting with those holding up to 10 million guaraníes (about US$1,600). Deposits are insured up to about US$37,000, which the central bank says covers nearly all of Ueno’s customers. It calls the collapse an isolated case and insists the broader financial system is safe.

Prosecutors have charged 27 people, including Ueno’s controlling shareholder, Miguel Vázquez, with crimes including breach of trust and attempted fraud, and six bank directors are in pretrial detention. Authorities have seized nine luxury cars from Vázquez’s home, along with a yacht and small planes linked to him, and searched executives’ homes in a gated community outside the capital.

Isabel Debre, Nayara Batschke and Emilio Sanabria, The Associated Press

DeBre reported from Salto, Uruguay, and Batschke from Montevideo, Uruguay.

items.title: Tesla pulls the plug on Cybertruck production
items.description: Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Tesla CEO Elon Musk introduces the Cybertruck at Tesla's design studio Thursday, Nov. 21, 2019, in Hawthorne, Calif. (AP Photo/Ringo H.W. Chiu)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales.
items.body:
Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks.

The move is a major retreat from what has been one of Musk’s pet projects. In an X post, Musk said the wind-down would let Tesla make more of the Cybercab, a robotaxi he has made central to the automaker’s autonomous-vehicle ambitions, but one that has yet to prove itself commercially.

The announcement comes at the end of a bruising week for Musk, as his record political spending of nearly half a billion dollars yielded little in Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections, with the vast majority of the Republican candidates he backed losing their races.

Combined, his companies were on track to lose more than US$180 billion in market capitalization for the week.

While it was not immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker’s Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the specialized components for the heavy, angular model.

In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the “best vehicle Tesla has ever made” and the wind-down the “end of an era.”

Tesla has been shifting its focus to robotics and autonomy, a transition analysts say comes at the expense of the electric-vehicle business it helped pioneer as Chinese rivals gain ground.

The U.S. EV maker began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the U.S. last year, down 48 per cent from 38,965 in 2024. Around the start of production in 2023, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units.

“It doesn’t make sense to keep it going when it’s not meeting its targets,” said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. “Every rational auto guy would say the same.”

“It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla’s balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves.”

Musk’s SpaceX was one of the model’s biggest customers last year and bought Cybertrucks worth US$131 million from Tesla in 2025 at list price, according to its IPO filing.

‘Cybertruck won’t go, can’t go’

Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Pickup truck purists mocked its angular design, and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe.

The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them — only to leave massive cracks in two of them.

During Cybertruck’s official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors GM.N and Ford F.N, saying “finally, the future will look like the future.”

But the model has struggled to meet those expectations. Tesla has issued 11 recalls for the Cybertruck since it went on sale in late 2023, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Some vehicles required physical repairs, while others were fixed with over-the-air software updates.

Automotive analyst Felipe Muñoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pickups from Ford and others have also flopped in the U.S. market.

“All of them lost the competition because electric pick ups aren’t popular in the U.S.,” Muñoz said.

But Cybertruck’s sharp-edged stainless-steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact.

“Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won’t go, can’t go,” former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said.

Musk’s new bet

The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk’s key bets in his push to turn Tesla into an AI and robotics company rather than just an automaker.

Musk has said he sees it as Tesla’s main autonomous model supplying a global network of robotaxis.

After years of delays to Musk’s self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September. However, the automaker still has to answer the U.S. auto safety agency’s questions on whether it has properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an audit in September to review the basis for that certification.

“Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab,” Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

However, the Cybercab is unlikely to make up for lost Cybertruck volumes soon. The two-seater robotaxi is still a small program, with production beginning only earlier this year. Tesla has listed an installed capacity of more than 125,000 units.

About 570 of the more than 1,200 Tesla robotaxis operating in Texas are Cybercabs, with the rest mainly Model Y vehicles, according to the state’s Department of Motor Vehicles.

items._ogDesc: Wall Street equities rallied, reversing course after trillions of dollars of world stock market value was wiped out over fears on regulations for the AI industry.
items.body:
NEW YORK/LONDON — Wall Street equities mostly rallied on Friday, reversing course after trillions of dollars of world stock market value was wiped out over fears that Democratic election victories this week would bring tighter U.S. regulations for the AI industry.

Benchmark S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were trading higher with technology, communication services and consumer discretionary stocks driving gains. The Dow edged lower on the day. All three indexes were on track for weekly losses following a brutal selloff in the prior session.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.08 per cent, the S&P 500 rose 0.71 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.4 per cent.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was up 4.2 per cent after slumping in its biggest one-day drop since April 2025. Nvidia rose three per cent, after suffering its worst day since January 2025, when the emergence of low-cost Chinese AI model DeepSeek hammered markets.

Other heavyweight chipmakers, including AMD, Intel, and Micron Technology, were up between 5.5 per cent and 10 per cent, while Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX were also up two and eight per cent respectively after losses earlier this week.

“Most of the disruption of the AI buildout will not probably occur but it’s just the uncertainty of the change in government from Republican-led to Democratic-led, not only at the federal level but the state, local levels,” said Gerry Sparrow, president and portfolio manager at Sparrow Capital Management.

“That’s causing some disruption in the expectations of investors... The volatility around elections or any political event, whether it be war or terrorist attack, is always going to disrupt the market.”

Texas’ Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said on Thursday that the state — which already has a large share of U.S. data centres — will introduce new laws to protect local communities from their further mass buildup.

The jitters are hitting an AI trade already under pressure from fears that the massive cost of the data centres and other infrastructure will limit future returns, spurring margin calls and spooking retail investors and hedge funds alike.

Ripple effect

The bounces were in stark contrast with market action in the rest of the world. Europe’s STOXX 600 lost one per cent. In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s KOSPI both slumped about six per cent. For the Nikkei — just like Wall Street the previous day — it was the biggest one-day drop since U.S. President Donald Trump’s “Liberation Day” trade tariff panic of April 2025.

  • Latest updates on investing here

The MSCI All-World index fell 0.52 per cent while MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan lost three per cent.

Payrolls beat forecasts

U.S. nonfarm payrolls, usually one of the most-focused on pieces of data, but largely overshadowed by the tech drama, showed a stronger-than-expected 165,000 pickup in jobs.

An anticipated slowdown in annual wage growth to below three per cent for the first time in nearly five and a half years did not materialize either as it came in at 3.1 per cent.

  • Latest updates on currencies here

The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note ticked up to 4.85 per cent, having dropped to its lowest level since Sept. 9 overnight.

In currencies, the dollar rose against major currencies including the euro, yen and Swiss franc. It was up 0.52 per cent against the yen and rose 0.47 per cent against the Swiss franc. The euro was down 0.68 per cent against the dollar at US$1.1142.

Brent crude prices LCOc1 tiptoed back up towards US$100 a barrel, but are still set for their biggest weekly drop since 2020 on hopes the midterms’ results might prompt Trump to de-escalate the Iran war.

items.title: Could the US’s blue wave bring an end to the Canada trade war?
items.description: Economist says Trump will face pressure to wind down tariff chaos, potentially signalling good news ahead for Canada’s housing outlook
items.content: <p>Economist says Trump will face pressure to wind down tariff chaos, potentially signalling good news ahead for Canada’s housing outlook</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639295080400390618.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Economist says Trump will face pressure to wind down tariff chaos, potentially signalling good news ahead for Canada’s housing outlook
items.body:
A Democratic Party wave swept the US on Tuesday, ending Republican control of both houses of Congress and potentially curbing Donald Trump’s ability to govern with the same force he’s used in the first half of his second presidency.

For Canada, the biggest immediate question is whether that political earthquake could put pressure on the Trump administration to revisit its controversial global tariff policy, one that’s weighed against the Canadian economy and damaged Canada’s housing market outlook.

Trump can still wield executive orders, a hallmark of his current presidency and one of the main ways he’s imposed and adjusted tariffs on key trading partners including Canada.

But he could face pressure from both outside and within his own party to wind back the levies on Canada – a development that would likely mark a major boost for the Canadian housing market.

On Thursday, Oxford Economics’ lead US economist Bernard Yaros highlighted how lawmakers could make ending the trade war with Canada a focus during the next Congress.

“There is widespread enough dissatisfaction in Congress with the US tariffs on Canada, given how important cross-border trade is between Canada and a lot of our northern border states,” he said.

“A lot of the fallout has been very visible for voters, especially on the ground in Maine where you’ve seen a big hit to the tourism industry from [fewer] Canadian arrivals ever since the breakout of the trade war between the US and Canada.”

How the trade war has damaged Canada’s housing market

High interest rates and affordability concerns have kept homebuyers on the sidelines across Canada in 2025 and 2026, but the outbreak of trade tensions with the US when Trump took office in January last year has also been a big factor in the market’s sluggishness.

Economists including BMO Capital Markets director and senior economist Sal Guatieri have flagged how the prolonged tariff dispute is damaging the housing market outlook and consumer confidence.

In September, Guatieri told CMP that the imposition of further tariffs could increase concerns about job security and push Canadians away from making a big investment in housing. “Until we see some clarity and de-escalation of trade tensions, I think the housing market could remain pretty fragile for a while,” he said.

The fall housing market has remained subdued partly because of deteriorating trade relations, according to Royal LePage.

The real estate giant’s president and chief executive officer Phil Soper said last month that while buyers have more negotiating power in a quieter market, other forces are denting their confidence.

“Unfortunately, it’s the economic uncertainty – both related to the trade war and the Iran war – that will likely keep a lot of buyers, especially first-time buyers, on the sidelines,” he said.

Talk of a potential deal intensifies

As the midterms neared, Trump suggested a deal with Canada could be close, perhaps indicting his awareness of how unpopular the tariff wave had been.

Prime minister Mark Carney, meanwhile, hinted at a return to the negotiating table – and Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) deputy chief economist Aled ab Iorwerth noted a trade deal could potentially brighten the outlook for home building and mortgage arrears.

Delinquencies have crept steadily higher across most markets, but tariff-impacted areas including Southern Ontario have been most heavily impacted.

South of the border, the Democrats will now command clear majorities in both the Senate and House – a fact that Yaros sees signalling a potential de-escalation ahead in trade tensions.

“The Canadian tariffs in particular are very unpopular,” he said. “We’ve seen already legislation attempting to repeal them. And I think with Democratic majorities, you could see renewed efforts.

“At the very least, that’s one area where we could actually see Congress force the administration to back down on tariffs. I think really the risks for a further flareup in North American trade relations is probably less on the other side of the midterms.”

items.title: Why Canadian mortgage brokers should not miss the CMAs
items.description: The Canadian Mortgage Awards return November 25 — here's what 20 years of recognition mean for you
items.content: <p>The Canadian Mortgage Awards return November 25 — here's what 20 years of recognition mean for you</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639295887034839033.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The Canadian Mortgage Awards return November 25 — here's what 20 years of recognition mean for you
items.body:
Twenty years ago, the Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) set out to do something the industry had never done at scale: name, in a room full of peers, the mortgage professionals who had genuinely earned the right to be called the best.

On November 25, that tradition continues at Rebel Toronto — and for brokers, lenders, and mortgage professionals across Canada who have not yet made plans to attend, the case for going has rarely been stronger.

The event spans 23 award categories covering everyone from individual brokers and business development managers (BDMs) to brokerages, underwriters, and lenders.

Its 2026 milestone marks two decades of setting the standard for excellence in Canadian mortgage, and the recognition it delivers carries real commercial and professional weight.

Recognition that moves markets and careers

For mortgage brokers and originators operating in an increasingly competitive Canadian lending market, a CMA nomination or win signals something to prospective clients, lenders, and referral partners that no advertising campaign can replicate: an independent, credible assessment that the work you are doing is among the best in the country.

Excellence awardees and winners are announced in CMP magazine and across its digital channels, reaching thousands of mortgage professionals nationwide. That coverage continues throughout the year, through online profiles and industry events, extending the value of recognition well beyond a single evening.

For past winners, the effect has been tangible. Steven Ranson of HomeEquity Bank, a previous CMA winner, described the award as a reflection of a career's worth of work.

Kyle Benzies of DLC AIMI Collective Mortgage Group noted that the recognition resonates directly with clients and has the potential to change the trajectory of a business. These are not uncommon reactions, they reflect the weight the industry has consistently assigned to the CMAs over two decades.

For brokerages, a win is also a tool for internal culture. Recognising the collective effort of underwriters, document specialists, and support teams alongside the brokers who face clients is the kind of acknowledgement that strengthens retention and reinforces what the firm stands for.

Secure a table at the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards and celebrate your team’s achievements alongside industry leaders, innovators, and top-performing professionals from across the country. #MortgageAwardsCA Book your table today: https://t.co/SSKx4yuft5 https://t.co/f31Lgyrrzt — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 28, 2026

A room worth being in

The CMAs draw hundreds of the foremost mortgage professionals and senior executives from top organisations across Canada every year.

For brokers who operate largely from their own offices or through aggregator networks, it is one of the few occasions where the full breadth of the industry — from originators to lenders to regulators — occupies the same space at the same time.

The networking value of that setting is structural, not incidental.

Relationship-driven businesses like mortgage broking are built over years, often through a handful of consequential conversations. An evening designed around the industry's most accomplished professionals is precisely the environment in which those conversations happen.

For brokers who are earlier in their careers, attendance carries a different kind of value: the ability to benchmark directly against those who have already been recognised as the country's best, to understand what distinguishes the work of a CMA winner from the field, and to begin building the relationships that determine where referrals and opportunities flow in the years ahead. 

A process built for credibility

One reason the CMAs have maintained their standing for 20 years is the integrity of the selection and judging process.

Nominations, which are open to all mortgage professionals and organisations from across Canada — including brokers, brokerages, lenders, BDMs, underwriters, agents, and service providers — are accepted from June 8 to August 14.

The CMA team then conducts independent research to supplement nominations, drawing on knowledge gathered through CMP, to ensure that deserving candidates are not overlooked because they did not self-nominate.

Excellence awardees — the shortlist — are announced in September, with judging conducted by an independent panel of mortgage and finance industry leaders in October and November 2026. Any judge with a conflict of interest in a category recuses themselves.

Winners are determined through a points-based aggregation of judges' votes, with the results revealed live at the gala on November 25. 

That structure matters for brokers assessing whether to enter or attend. Recognition earned through a process this transparent carries more weight with clients and business partners than self-reported rankings and it is the reason a CMA win has become a signal the industry genuinely trusts.

items._ogDesc: Canada's employment stalled in October as the unemployment rate climbed to 6.7%. StatCan warns nearly 1 in 3 adults now struggle to afford basic necessities.
items.body:
Canadian employment was little changed last month, but the details were more concerning. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data show employment stalled in October, but unemployment climbed. It’s not just harder to find a job, but those unemployed are struggling to find work. The agency warns that nearly 1 in 3 adults now face financial hardship, rolling back gains made since 2022.

Canadian Employment Stalls As Unemployment Climbs

Canadian seasonally adjusted unemployment rate.

Employment was virtually flat (0%; -4.7k) in October, following losses in September (-68k) and August (-42k). Despite the stall, more people searching for work pushed the unemployment rate to 6.7%, up 0.2 points. Most of the pain is concentrated in Alberta and Ontario, where the rate is now 7.3% in both provinces.

October’s flat move somewhat downplays the emerging weakness in the labour force. A sharp drop in private sector employment (-53k) was only offset by a jump in the public sector (+50k). The public sector’s increase comes after four months of losses.

Employment has only grown 0.1% (+17k) over the past year. That’s a little light considering population revisions show 189.4k more people y/y in Q3. StatCan has previously stated that the revisions will be gradually introduced into employment data. Dismissing slow growth due to the population no longer makes sense, and unemployment is understated.

Retail Leads Job Losses, While Construction Adds Workers

The areas most impacted were wholesale and retail (-1.0%; -29k jobs) in October, contracting 3.7% (-113k) in the past year. Those losses were partially offset by construction growing 0.9% (+16k) in October, rising 2.9% (+47k) in the past year.

One surprise in the data is education, which grew 1.0% (+15k) in October. This partially reverses the 35k jobs lost in the sector in September, but it remains 3.0% (-48k) lower than last year.

Nearly 30% Of Canadians Struggle to Cover Necessities

The share of Canadians who struggled to pay for necessities, including transportation, housing, food, and clothing.

A lot more Canadians are struggling, according to StatCan’s special supplement. The agency’s labour report also had numbers on the share of those aged 15+ struggling to pay for necessities. They found 29.7% of people had difficulty paying for necessities in the past four weeks, up 2 points from last year. This recent bump partially rolls back improvements made from 2022 through 2025.

Among Canada’s 15 CMAs, the worst hit is Oshawa, where 38.4% of people struggled to buy necessities. It was followed by Windsor (36.9%) and Hamilton (35.9%). The trio makes it easy to conclude this is trade war-related, but it may be an Ontario thing. Even more diversified regions like Toronto (32%) were much higher than Vancouver (26.1%). Though, to be fair, 1 in 4 adults struggling to pay for necessities is still a systemic failure.

Struggling to find a job after a loss is definitely a contributor. Only 18.9% of those unemployed in September found work in October, well below the 24.6% in the same period from 2017 to 2019. Long-term unemployment (27+ weeks) also hit 23.7%, up from 21.5% last year and an average of just 17.2% between 2017 and 2019, warns StatCan.

Headline employment shows a stall, but clearly that’s an overly optimistic view. The population continues to grow faster than the handful of jobs being created. Replacing a lost job is harder, and long-term unemployment is spreading to more people. Add to that the reversal in financial security improvements, and this is one of the worst reports in a while.

items.title: Ottawa proposes Bank Act changes to widen banking competition
items.description: Budget 2026 targets the Big Six with new ownership thresholds and $250,000 deposit insurance
items.content: <p>Budget 2026 targets the Big Six with new ownership thresholds and $250,000 deposit insurance</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639295829822671112.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Budget 2026 targets the Big Six with new ownership thresholds and $250,000 deposit insurance
items.body:
The Carney government’s Budget 2026 has placed Canada’s concentrated banking sector under direct pressure, proposing Bank Act amendments that would give mid-sized lenders and credit unions a credible path to growth in a market long dominated by the Big Six.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne’s budget documents propose lifting the equity threshold at which banks must adopt widely held ownership structures from $12 billion to $25 billion, giving challenger institutions considerably more room to scale before any obligation to open their shareholder base applies.

Raising the bar for mid-sized lenders

Additional measures include exempting foreign bank subsidiaries with less than $8 billion in equity from the public holding requirement, provided the parent institution is widely held and listed on a recognised foreign stock exchange.

A statutory one-year timeline for new entrants into the federal financial institutions framework would also be introduced, alongside greater ownership flexibility for mid-sized banks.

For mortgage brokers, the competitive stakes are concrete. Brokers command a 33% share of the Canadian mortgage market – up four percentage points since 2022, according to Mortgage Professionals Canada’s 2024 Mid-Year Report – and a wider lender field typically delivers better rates and more product diversity for clients.

Naga Parvatharajan, chief executive of Ratehub.ca in Canada, has described Canada’s current regulatory direction as a genuine opportunity.

Speaking on Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI)’s streamlined approvals framework for new lenders entering the market, he said the approach was “exactly the kind of structural signal that tells fintech innovators, consumers and incumbents: this market is open for business.”

He added that “when more institutions enter the market, Canadians gain better rates and innovative options,” and stressed the need for follow-through: “This is a meaningful step forward, but now we must ensure the entire ecosystem evolves in tandem.”

The budget further proposes giving the OSFI a new secondary competition objective, requiring the regulator to weigh proportionality and compliance burden in its supervisory decisions.

Proposed amendments would also allow provincial credit unions to acquire federal credit unions directly.

Deposit insurance set to double

Beyond ownership reform, the government is proposing to raise Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation (CDIC) coverage from $100,000 to $250,000 per account.

Temporary protection for high balances linked to specific life events, including home sale proceeds, would also apply, with caps on eligible registered and tax-free account deposits removed entirely.

As CMP’s breakdown of Budget 2026’s biggest housing announcements for brokers detailed, these reforms sit alongside a broader lending and insurance overhaul.

items.content: <p>Ottawa pledges $45B for housing and raises the optional insurance cap to $1.5M</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639295802434056184.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Ottawa pledges $45B for housing and raises the optional insurance cap to $1.5M
items.body:
The Carney government tabled Budget 2026 on November 5, releasing a broad set of housing measures spanning mortgage insurance, the foreign buyer ban, and new funding commitments that will shape conversations between brokers and their clients across Canada.

The big numbers: $45 billion and 200,000 homes

The centrepiece is a $45-billion total capitalisation of Build Canada Homes (BCH), comprising the $13 billion committed in Budget 2025 plus a new $13-billion injection beginning in 2027–28.

Ottawa says BCH is on track to produce approximately 200,000 homes over the next decade, with a target to triple annual non-market housing starts to 24,000.

RBC assistant chief economist Cynthia Leach, speaking ahead of the budget, described the task as “less about new programs and more about disciplined execution,” noting that federal housing spending is set to decline sharply as existing programmes expire.

BMO Capital Markets added separately that “near-term inflation trends and any resolution of the trade dispute will matter more for both yields and the loonie” than the headline housing figures. 

Stephanie Shewchuk, housing policy lead at RBC Thought Leadership in Toronto, previously said that maintaining buyer confidence requires the government to resolve outstanding details quickly

“When people are making decisions about probably maybe the biggest purchase they will ever make, they want the details to be clear,” Shewchuk said.

“Otherwise, they start to develop more of a wait-and-see approach, and you lose some of the momentum.” 

Mortgage rules, insurance, and the foreign buyer ban

Ottawa proposes raising the home price ceiling for optional mortgage insurance from $1 million to $1.5 million, giving buyers with a 20% deposit on higher-priced properties access to a wider range of lender offers and potentially more competitive rates.

No start date has been confirmed; a 30-year amortisation applies only where at least one borrower is a first-time buyer or the property is newly built.

From February 1, 2027, triplexes and fourplexes will qualify under new insurance rules, with construction loans insurable for up to 90% of projected completed value.

Private insurers will also be permitted to compete with the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) on loans for buildings of five to 50 units.

The federal proposal to extend the ban on foreign purchases of existing homes runs to January 1, 2029, with new residential properties exempted to stimulate preconstruction activity.

National Bank of Canada (NBC) chief economist Stéphane Marion recently said he believed the ban was undermining investment appeal: “How can you pretend to be a standout investor again if you tell foreign buyers you can’t touch the residential market in Canada?” 

For brokers, the most closely watched measure may be the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) income verification pilot, backed by $13 million over three years with testing starting in 2027–28.

Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) says it will continue pressing for direct broker and brokerage access – which remains unresolved since consultations began in late 2024.

Federal deposit insurance is also proposed to rise from $100,000 to $250,000.

items.description: Market pricing for a follow-up move in January has already retreated to 77% from 96% the day before the release
items.content: <p>Market pricing for a follow-up move in January has already retreated to 77% from 96% the day before the release</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639295754536058459.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Market pricing for a follow-up move in January has already retreated to 77% from 96% the day before the release
items.body:
Canada’s labour market shed 4,700 jobs in October, pushing the national unemployment rate to 6.7% from 6.5%,  a third consecutive month of deterioration that is now complicating the Bank of Canada’s (BoC) path to a December rate hike.

Statistics Canada released the figures on November 6, with the result significantly undershooting analyst expectations of a 13,600-job gain.

The data arrived less than two weeks after the BoC raised its overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.50% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023.

Market pricing for a follow-up move in January has already retreated to 77% from 96% the day before the release, according to TD Economics.

A labour market still losing ground

Beneath the headline figure, the composition of job losses told a more troubling story.

Full-time employment fell by 18,100 positions while private-sector employment declined by 52,500, a sharp contrast to public-sector gains of 49,600.

The services sector shed 25,300 jobs, with wholesale and retail trade accounting for the bulk of the damage at 29,000 losses.

Construction added 16,000 jobs and educational services contributed 15,000 on the goods-producing side, according to Statistics Canada.

The result builds on the strain that economists flagged after Canada’s September jobs shock and what it meant for rates, when the economy shed 68,300 positions, its worst month of 2026.

Andrew Hencic, Director & Senior Economist at TD Economics in Toronto, characterised the report as a continuation of a worsening trend.

“We’re now at three months and counting for downbeat labour market reports,” he wrote.

“Ongoing labour force growth means there is growing slack in the labour market. Reinforcing the notion is the ongoing weakness in average hourly earnings — a signal that labour demand is not yet outstripping supply.”

Average hourly wages rose 2.2% year-over-year in October, easing from 2.3% in September.

The job-finding rate sat at 18.9%, well below its 2017–2019 average of 24.6%, according to TD Economics.

Hencic noted the central question now is whether businesses can pass on higher costs in an environment of weak wage growth.

Not all readings pointed uniformly downward. Claire Fan, Senior Economist at RBC Economics in Toronto, noted that prime-age unemployment held steady at 5.6% in October, with weakness concentrated elsewhere.

“Weakness was concentrated in the 15 to 24 year cohort, where the unemployment rate rose sharply to 13.7%, driven by both lower employment and rising labour force participation,” Fan wrote in a research note released following the data.

She also pushed back on concerns that US tariffs were accelerating broad job losses.

“New U.S. tariffs implemented since August 22 have not, and are not expected to lead to widespread layoffs in Canada,” Fan wrote.

“They are severe but of a narrow scope.”

Her outlook was cautiously constructive: “Our forecast expects the unemployment rate in Canada to keep edging lower, to below 6% in the second half of 2027.”

What it means for brokers ahead of December 9

The October rate hike has already deepened broker concerns over Canada’s struggling housing market.

For brokers navigating clients through Canada’s mounting 2026 mortgage renewal pressures, the December 9 decision carries immediate practical consequences.

Jessica Rickerby, president of the Canadian Mortgage Brokers Association of Ontario (CMBA Ontario), said the data reinforces the view that the affordability crisis demands urgent attention. “While inflation is a key concern of Ontarians, so is housing affordability,” Rickerby said. “The difference is that affordability is a pressing issue right now, whereas inflation is — at present — a hypothetical.”

items.title: Canadian government to extend – but loosen – foreign homebuyer ban
items.description: Budget proposes to keep measure in place until the start of 2029, but exempt new residential properties
items.content: <p>Budget proposes to keep measure in place until the start of 2029, but exempt new residential properties</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639295149895933608.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Budget proposes to keep measure in place until the start of 2029, but exempt new residential properties
items.body:
The federal government has proposed an extension of the ban on non-resident foreign homebuyers for a further two years, but says it would exclude new residential properties from the policy.

Thursday’s federal budget revealed that the government intends to renew the measure until January 1, 2029 – but the proposed amendment has sparked speculation that it may be attempting to drum up purchase activity in the preconstruction sector, where investor demand has plunged in recent years.

Extending and adjusting the measure, the government said, “would help protect housing affordability by keeping the vast majority of the market available for Canadians, while unlocking additional investment in new housing supply.”

The government said it would support other policy measures to address housing market pressures “including speculation” and unveiled separate housing proposals including billions in additional funding for housing.

Finance minister François-Philippe Champagne’s statement also included a pledge to introduce more affordable mortgages, a proposal that will spur plenty of debate in the mortgage industry.

The budget said it was “establishing new regulations to enhance publicly available information on insured mortgage rates, allowing more Canadians to compare and shop for the best available rates.”

Its proposed investment in housing will total an additional $44.7 billion over the next 11 years, which it claimed would end homelessness within a decade and build a more affordable housing market.

Homebuyer ban a hot-button industry issue

The ban on non-resident buyers was first proposed during the federal election campaign in 2021 and enacted by then-prime minister Justin Trudeau, coming into force at the beginning of 2023.

It’s won wide support within the mortgage industry, although the housing market slowdown of recent years has seen prominent real estate professionals call for the government to scrap or amend the policy.

Last year, a Research Co. poll showed around 76% of Canadians support the measure, but National Bank of Canada (NBC) chief economist Stéphane Marion recently argued that the ban is detrimental to Canada’s efforts to attract more foreign investment.

“How can you pretend to be a standout investor again if you tell foreign buyers you can’t touch the residential market in Canada?” Marion said.

The post Vancouver Real Estate Prices Slip, Just 3% Higher Than 2017 Peak appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Vancouver real estate prices are sliding into a second-leg correction, with home values now sitting just 3% higher than the 2017 peak.
items.body:
Vancouver real estate prices are diving into a second-leg correction. Greater Vancouver Realtors (GVREB) data shows home prices fell further in October. Strong inventory and weak sales are driving one of the sharpest corrections in Canada, with prices now just 3% higher than they were 9 years ago.

Vancouver Home Prices Up Just 3% Since 2017

The price of a typical home across Greater Vancouver.

Source: GVREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

The price of a typical home fell 0.7% (-$7.3k) to $1.07 million in October, 5.2% (-$58.5k) lower than last year. Since the 2022 peak, they’ve plunged 14.7% (-$184.2k) to the weakest level since March 2021. While prices initially resisted a Toronto-sized correction, they’ve consistently been grinding lower. As of last month, prices were just 3.1% (+$32.5k) higher than the 2017 cycle peak. That’s pretty much 9 years of stagnation.

Vancouver Home Sales Fall To Correction Levels

Greater Vancouver existing home sales.

Source: GVREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

The demand slump continued, with the board reporting just 2,024 sales in October, 10.2% lower than last year. October sales are never high, but this scale of weakness is rare outside of market slumps. It’s a level consistent with those in 2022, 2018, and 2012—not exactly years the industry is longing to relive.

Vancouver New Listings Slip, But Overall Inventory Remains Strong

Fewer sellers hit the market last month. There were 4,805 new listings in October, down 11.6% from last year and a 3-year low for the month. However, lower doesn’t mean low—this is a surprisingly healthy volume for the region. It’s an elevated level that’s rarely seen outside of slumps.

Vancouver Real Estate Inventory Remains Unusually Strong

Active listings of homes for sale across Greater Vancouver.

Source: GVREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

Stagnating inventory may be part of the reason no one’s in a rush to list their home for sale. There were 15,688 active listings in October, down 4.3% from last year, when the market set a 13-year high for the month. To be blunt, the drop was from a very high place, and still marked one of the highest volumes on record. The downward pressure on prices was further amplified by the fact that sales dropped at a faster rate.

Home prices in Greater Vancouver are having a crisis of value. While the market didn’t drop to the same extent as Toronto, it also failed three attempts to move higher. Buyers in the region are resistant to higher prices, and it’s unclear how much prices need to fall to get them to jump in. Meanwhile, the market is approaching nearly 10 years of stagnation.

items.title: ‘We’re close to the bottom’: Private market gets ready to turn the page
items.description: Real estate lawyer says the worst of the private lending turbulence may be over for mortgage brokers
items.content: <p>Real estate lawyer says the worst of the private lending turbulence may be over for mortgage brokers</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639294998909890808.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Real estate lawyer says the worst of the private lending turbulence may be over for mortgage brokers
items.body:
Canada’s private lending market is approaching a turning point – and the difficult conditions that have defined recent years may be the very thing that sets it up for a more stable future, according to a real estate lawyer who’s worked through its transformation.

Daniele Grechi (pictured top), partner and founder of Grechi Carter Real Estate Lawyers, told Canadian Mortgage Professional the worst of the current cycle may be behind it as the mortgage industry prepares to usher in a new year in 2027.

“My general thoughts are we’re close to the bottom. Hopefully things are going to move up from here,” he said. The sector will be in a better space for withstanding the turbulence of recent times, according to Grechi: “It’s really forced people to have tighter processes. I think tough times make for better actions and people have had to tighten their processes, really look at their underwriting.”

The sector has faced the same challenges as the wider industry amid a slower purchase market, climbing interest rates, economic uncertainty, and rising mortgage strain in certain pockets.

But the progress made in private lending over the past decade and a half shouldn’t be understated, Grechi said, with the sector increasingly moving into the mainstream and pivoting away from its status as an option of last resort.

“In the first six or seven years, it was such a different space,” he said. “It was a lot of syndicate lending, a lot less structure, a lot of random different groups, small lenders – and the returns were just absurd for the risk levels that were available.”

Annual property value increases of around 20% in the early days made the space an easy – and lucrative – one to operate in, attracting a surge of capital and a wide range of participants.

How COVID changed the game

A turning point arrived during the COVID-19 pandemic, when institutional investors flooded into the private lending market in significant numbers. Grechi said the process, rigour and competitive pressure that those companies brought have redefined the space entirely.

“What we’ve seen is the flock of institutional money through the MICs [mortgage investment corporations] and they very much have professionalized the space,” he said. “What we now refer to as private is kind of institutional, very regulated, very professional, extremely competitive. I think that’s the biggest change I’ve seen since we started in the business.”

That progress isn’t to say that the sector is an entirely safe bet. In its latest residential mortgage industry report, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) highlighted that what it labels mortgage investment entities (MIEs) are showing the strongest signs of stress among lenders, mainly because they’re more exposed to higher-risk borrowers than other institutions.

Risk among MIEs/MICs is especially concentrated in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA), CMHC said, with the share of MIE balances in arrears for 90 days or more jumping from 3% in 2023’s third quarter to 11.1% by the first quarter of 2026 in that region.

But that segment represents “only a small part” of the market, the national housing agency added, with certain MICs likely at greater exposure than others in the current climate.

Executives within the space have highlighted the likelihood of further consolidation as smaller MICs with riskier exposures continue to struggle in a turbulent market.

“Increased regulation is making it more difficult for smaller players to compete,” Brad Rembold, chief executive officer of All Island Equity MIC, told CMP in May. “This isn’t necessarily a bad thing – just a reality of the regulatory world we live in.”

What brokers are focusing on in their private lending conversations

Conversations with mortgage brokers, Grechi said, typically revolve around familiar priorities: speed, turnaround, and the ability to handle complex files. But tougher conditions have also impacted how brokers approach lender selection, reflecting a market where matching the right private lender to the right file is now a key skill for brokers.

“Not every lender is doing every deal anymore, so you’ve got to go to different lenders for different needs,” Grechi said. “You’ve got to know your sweet spots for whatever it is that your clients need.”

 A monthly report from Rentals.
items._ogDesc: TORONTO — The average asking price for a rental unit across Canada in October was $2,036, down 3.2 per cent compared with a year ago. A monthly report from Rentals.
items.body:
TORONTO — The average asking price for a rental unit across Canada in October was $2,036, down 3.2 per cent compared with a year ago.

A monthly report from Rentals.ca and Urbanation says October's decrease marks the smallest year-over-year decline since February, when rents were down 2.8 per cent from the same month a year earlier.

Average asking rents have now fallen year-over-year for 25 consecutive months, with prices down 5.4 per cent compared with two years ago and reaching their lowest October level since 2022.

Rents were essentially flat on a monthly basis, edging 0.1 per cent higher from September.

Urbanation president Shaun Hildebrand says the window for cheaper rents is closing in Toronto and Vancouver as prices are starting to rise for the first time in nearly three years amid declining supply, while renters still hold the advantage in Calgary, Edmonton and much of Ontario, where prices continue to fall.

Asking rents for purpose-built apartments fell 2.1 per cent year-over-year to an average of $2,040 last month, while asking rents for condominium apartments decreased 5.5 per cent to $2,048.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.
